title: Zenith Health - Private VPC Discovery
summary: Discovery focused on private/VPC deployment options for Redwood Private. Customer needs VPC peering or private endpoints, control plane networking, region constraints (US/EU), KMS integration, and audit logging. Agreed next steps: share private deployment network diagram, security/compliance pack, and schedule technical deep dive for pilot in us-east-1.
topics: Control plane networking and customer-managed routing
KMS/HSM and encryption at rest/in transit

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO - Zenith), James Lin (Head of Infra), Asha Kapoor (Security), Tom Rivers (ML Eng)

[00:00] Laura Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today, really appreciate it. Quick roll call and then we'll jump into your current networking constraints and goals.
[00:12] Maya Patel: Thanks Laura, yeah hi all. We're evaluating options for private deployment, we want to run in our VPCs, meet PHI requirements for a subset of workloads.
[00:20] James Lin: Hey, big thing for us is we need private connectivity, no public endpoints. We want either VPC peering or PrivateLink style endpoints, and we need the control plane to respect our CIDR ranges and not require wide open egress.
[00:34] Daniel Ortiz: Got it. To align expectations, Redwood Private offers a private control plane option that can be customer-managed networking. There are a few patterns: VPC peering across accounts, AWS PrivateLink (Private endpoints), and in some cases a managed VPC with VPN/Transit Gateway. Which of those are you leaning towards?
[00:48] James Lin: Ideally PrivateLink or an endpoint so traffic never goes over the internet. VPC peering is also ok but cross-account peering routes can be messy with our transit gateway setup.
[00:57] Asha Kapoor: On the security side we also need to understand KMS integration for key management, audit logs retention, and SSO mapping for RBAC. SOC2 evidence too.
[01:08] Laura Chen: Absolutely. We'll share our security pack. On KMS, Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest; for HSM-backed keys we have integrations via customer KMS aliases. We'll include the integration guide.
[01:22] Tom Rivers: Quick question — what about region constraints? We're multi-region (us-east-1 and eu-west-1) and for latency sensitive models we prefer to keep inference in-region. Can Redwood Private run in both regions?
[01:34] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, we can deploy in multiple regions, but for Private deployments it's typically an instance per region. We need to provision control plane components and serving nodes in each region. Inter-region replication for cache is optional but adds complexity. For initial pilot we usually recommend starting in a single region — us-east-1 — then expand.
[01:50] Maya Patel: If we start in us-east-1, will we be able to expand to eu-west-1 later with the same VPC patterns or will we need different networking approaches?
[01:59] Daniel Ortiz: The patterns translate, but things like VPC peering are region-specific. For EU you may prefer PrivateLink endpoints per region or use TGW for connectivity. We'll include a notes doc about inter-region routing and transit gateway compat.
[02:14] James Lin: Another practical concern is private DNS and endpoint discovery. If we use PrivateLink, how do we route DNS? Will Redwood provide private hostnames that resolve inside our VPC?
[02:27] Laura Chen: We provide private endpoint hostnames for PrivateLink deployments and we can share the zone names. For peering models, you control route tables and DNS resolution via cross-account resolver rules — we'll document recommended settings.
[02:40] Asha Kapoor: Any talk about egress for model downloads or updates? We have strict egress controls, no social internet access from our subnets.
[02:48] Daniel Ortiz: Model artifacts can be pulled via S3 access through VPC endpoints (gateway endpoints) or via direct peering; Redwood can stage artifacts in a customer S3 bucket if needed. We'll show the recommended secure artifact pull flow in the diagram.
[02:59] Maya Patel: Great. For audit logs we need to retain request logs 1 year and show per-request metadata. Is that supported?
[03:08] Laura Chen: Yes — audit logs with configurable retention are part of the private offering; we can ship logs to your S3 or to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose. We'll include specifics and sample IAM roles.

[03:30] (Transcript jump; mid-discussion on topology)
[03:30] James Lin: On IP usage — what are ENI counts and ephemeral IP usage per instance? We have limits on IPs per subnet and will need guidance for subnet sizing.
[03:40] Daniel Ortiz: Serving nodes attach ENIs for networking; typical small pool uses X ENIs but it varies by instance. For planning, we provide a subnet sizing doc; for heavy throughput we recommend /20-ish subnets to start. We'll attach that.
[03:55] Tom Rivers: Any idea on NAT gateway egress charges if we have to egress to S3? Could be costy.
[04:03] Laura Chen: We can avoid NAT egress by using VPC gateway endpoints for S3 and by keeping traffic internal via peering/private endpoints; we'll outline cost tradeoffs in the guidance.

[04:30] Maya Patel: Let's talk failure modes — if Redwood's control plane needs to reach the customer VPC, do we require open inbound from Redwood IP ranges?
[04:39] Daniel Ortiz: No, typically Rico — sorry — we rely on customer-managed endpoints. For PrivateLink, the endpoint is inside your VPC and we don't need broad inbound. For peering, route tables allow traffic. For control plane tasks that need call-home we can use a short-lived management channel through an egress-only path, however many customers prefer a fully customer-initiated connection pattern. We'll provide details.
[04:58] Asha Kapoor: For compliance, do you support isolated log storage and access controls (no Redwood engineers by default)?
[05:05] Laura Chen: Yes, RBAC and least privilege are standard; engineers can't access customer data without explicit session requests and audit trails. We'll include the org-level RBAC docs.

[05:30] (Later — more technical)
[05:30] Daniel Ortiz: A few technical notes: if you use VPC peering, you need to propagate routes and avoid overlapping CIDRs. For PrivateLink, we use NLBs behind the service and you create interface endpoints in your subnets. PrivateLink is generally simpler for cross-account, but it can be more expensive and requires managing interface endpoints in each AZ.
[05:51] James Lin: Any limitations on PrivateLink for cross-region?
[05:56] Daniel Ortiz: PrivateLink endpoints are region-specific — you'd need endpoints in each region. For cross-region traffic we'd recommend TGW or VPN. We'll include recommended architecture patterns for multi-region.

[06:20] Tom Rivers: Let's also cover metrics and latency — if we run in our VPC in us-east-1, what kind of p99 latency should we expect for small gen models?
[06:30] Daniel Ortiz: Typical p50/p95/p99 depends on instance type and batching; for small LLMs on g4dn-like infra you'll see p50 ~30–80ms, p99 depends on burst and batching. For enterprise workloads we size pools to hit your SLOs; the PoC will capture realistic numbers.
[06:47] Maya Patel: Ok. Timeline — we'd like a pilot for PHI workloads in a sandbox VPC in us-east-1 in the next 2–4 weeks. Is that realistic?
[06:56] Laura Chen: Yes, feasible. Next step is Redwood sends a PoC checklist, network template, and security pack. Then we schedule the SE deep dive to work through terraform/VPC configs with James.

[07:12] (Silence, notes)
[07:20] James Lin: On routing — do you support prefix lists so we can easily allow Redwood ranges in our NACLs?
[07:27] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, we publish Redwood-managed prefix lists for control plane egress when needed; for PrivateLink those are less required. We'll include the prefix list.

[10:00] (Mid-call, clarification and some transcription noise)
[10:00] Maya Patel: Sorry, quick thing — our compliance team will want to verify data residency for EU. If we expand to eu-west-1, can Redwood ensure no data crosses back to US accounts?
[10:15] Daniel Ortiz: Yes — when deployed per-region we can keep data and logs in-region. We'll provide the deployment manifest options to pin region and storage locations. There is some control plane metadata that may be replicated for health checks but we'll show options to restrict that.

[20:45] Asha Kapoor: Encryption — does Redwood support customer-managed keys for both storage and transit TLS?
[20:53] Laura Chen: Storage: yes, CMK. Transit: we use TLS; if you require mutual TLS we can discuss mutual auth on NLBs for PrivateLink. We'll include the MTLs note. (transcription: M T L S sometimes written as multi T S)

[30:00] (Later section, objections and pricing)
[30:05] James Lin: One of our concerns is cost of dedicated infra vs hosted. For dedicated pools, what's the minimal commit and how's failover handled?
[30:15] Laura Chen: For Redwood Dedicated/Private, reserved capacity commitments vary by region; pilot is opt-in with limited commit. Failover is via multi-AZ pools and automatic routing to fallback models; if you're using PrivateLink, routing is controlled on your side so failover patterns are documented. We'll share a pricing sheet and example commit sizes.

[40:12] (End of call wrap up)
[40:12] Laura Chen: To recap: Redwood will share the private deployment network diagram, prefix lists, security pack (SOC2/ISO), and a PoC checklist. We'll schedule a technical deep dive week of 2025-03-17. Customer will send region list and compliance questions. Anything to add?
[40:25] Maya Patel: That's accurate. Also want the subnet sizing doc and sample terraform for PrivateLink endpoints.
[40:32] Daniel Ortiz: I'll prepare a terraform snippet and sample route table changes.
[40:37] Asha Kapoor: Please include KMS integration steps and audit log retention policy in the pack.
[40:44] Laura Chen: Absolutely. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite.
[40:50] (Meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: there are a few minor speaker attribution issues and some automated transcription mistakes around acronyms (MTLS/M TLS/KMS sometimes split).
